Getting started with rk8s

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

rk8s is an R client for the Kubernetes API. It has two layers:

  • A high-level verb API — kube_get(), kube_apply(), kube_logs(), kube_watch(), … This is what most users want. You never have to type V1Deployment$new(...) to do everyday work.
  • A low-level typed/generated API — CoreV1Api, AppsV1Api, V1Pod, V1Deployment, … 944 operations and 635 model classes generated from the Kubernetes OpenAPI spec, mirroring the official Python client and Go client-go. There when you need it.

A Watch helper, Informer/Lister for client-go-style controllers, DynamicClient for CustomResources, pod_exec() / pod_port_forward(), and run_as_leader() for leader election sit alongside both layers.

Installing 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ian-flores/rk8s")

Authenticating 

library(rk8s)
k <- kube()                                   # $KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config
# k <- kube(context = "my-dev")
# k <- kube(config_file = "~/configs/prod.yaml")
# k <- kube(namespace = "my-app")             # override the context namespace

Inside a pod running as a ServiceAccount:

k <- kube(client = ApiClient$new(load_incluster_config()))

load_kube_config() reads kubeconfigs the way kubectl does: a KUBECONFIG list of several files (merged, first definition wins), the context’s default namespace, bearer tokens and token files, basic auth, client certificates (inline or as files relative to the kubeconfig that names them), exec credential plugins (EKS’s aws-iam-authenticator, GKE’s gke-gcloud-auth-plugin, AKS’s kubelogin, any OIDC helper), the oidc auth-provider with token refresh, proxy-url, tls-server-name and insecure-skip-tls-verify.

Requests that hit API throttling (429) are retried for any method; server errors (500-504) and dropped connections are retried for reads only. Set Configuration$max_retries (default 3) to change this.

The verb API

Resource references can be:

  • a kind alias: "pod", "pods", "po", "deploy", "svc", "ing", "crd", …
  • "kind/name": "deployment/nginx"
  • explicit "apiVersion:Kind": "apps/v1:Deployment"
  • a c(apiVersion, Kind) vector: c("apps/v1", "Deployment")

The examples below assume a pod called nginx-abc and, after the apply section, a Deployment called nginx.

Get / list 

kube_get(k, "pods", namespace = "default")              # list
kube_get(k, "pod", "nginx-abc")                          # single
kube_get(k, "deployment/nginx")                          # alt syntax
kube_get(k, "pods", label_selector = "app=nginx")
kube_get(k, "apps/v1:Deployment", "nginx")               # explicit GVK

kube_get() returns an rk8s_object (single) or rk8s_list (collection). kube_list() pages through large collections for you. A built-in as.data.frame() method gives you a tabular view:

pods <- kube_get(k, "pods")
head(as.data.frame(pods))
#>     namespace                    name kind     age   status
#> 1     default                  nginx-1  Pod    12m  Running
#> 2     default                  nginx-2  Pod    12m  Running
#> 3 kube-system          coredns-abc-xyz  Pod      4h  Running

Apply (server-side apply)

kube_apply() accepts a path, a YAML/JSON string, an R list, or a generated model. Multi-document YAML works — each document is routed to the correct endpoint via discovery:

# From a file
kube_apply(k, "deployment.yaml")

# From an R list (the most natural form for programmatic generation)
kube_apply(k, list(
  apiVersion = "v1", kind = "ConfigMap",
  metadata = list(name = "demo"),
  data = list(hello = "world")
))

# From a multi-doc YAML string
kube_apply(k, "
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: demo-cm}
data: {greeting: hello}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: demo-svc}
spec:
  selector: {app: demo}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8080}]
")

# Force-take ownership of conflicting fields (server-side apply force):
kube_apply(k, "deployment.yaml", force = TRUE)

Field manager defaults to "rk8s"; override with field_manager =.

Delete, scale, logs, watch 

kube_scale(k, "deployment", "nginx", replicas = 5)
kube_scale(k, "statefulset/postgres", replicas = 3)

cat(kube_logs(k, "nginx-abc", tail = 50))
kube_logs(k, "nginx-abc", container = "sidecar", follow = TRUE)

w <- kube_watch(k, "pods",
  on_event = function(type, obj) {
    message(type, " ", obj$metadata$name)
    TRUE  # keep watching; return FALSE to stop
  },
  timeout_seconds = 30
)
w$end_reason   # "stop", "timeout" or "gone" (resourceVersion too old)

kube_delete(k, "pod", "nginx-abc")
kube_delete(k, "deployment/nginx", grace_period = 0)

timeout_seconds is a wall-clock limit: the watch reconnects after server-side timeouts but returns once the time is up.

Anything custom

kube_apply() works for CRs out of the box (any apiVersion+kind), and kube_get() resolves them via the dynamic client. So a typical controller is:

foos <- kube_list(k, "example.com/v1:Foo", namespace = "default")
for (f in foos$items) {
  if (is.null(f$status$ready) || !isTRUE(f$status$ready)) {
    kube_apply(k, list(
      apiVersion = "example.com/v1", kind = "Foo",
      metadata = list(name = f$metadata$name),
      status = list(ready = TRUE)
    ))
  }
}

Watching with a local cache: Informer + Lister

When you want to react to changes without re-listing the API server every tick, use Informer. One watch feeds an in-memory cache plus your event handlers; Lister gives you O(1) lookups. The initial list is paged, and if the watch falls too far behind (410 Gone) the informer lists again and reconciles its cache, firing on_delete for anything removed in the meantime.

inf <- Informer$new(
  k$client,
  resource_path = "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods",
  object_from_list = V1Pod$from_list
)
inf$add_event_handler(
  on_add    = function(obj) message("add: ", obj$metadata$name),
  on_update = function(old, new) {
    if (!identical(old$status$phase, new$status$phase))
      message(new$metadata$name, ": ",
              old$status$phase, " -> ", new$status$phase)
  },
  on_delete = function(obj) message("gone: ", obj$metadata$name)
)
inf$run(stop_seconds = 120)

pods <- inf$lister()
pods$get("nginx-abc", namespace = "default")   # cache lookup, no API call
pods$list()

Exec and port-forward

Run a command in a pod and collect its output:

r <- pod_exec(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", c("ls", "-la", "/"))
cat(r$stdout)
r$exit_code

# With stdin
pod_exec(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", "cat", stdin_data = "hi\n")$stdout

For an interactive session use pod_exec_open(), which returns a PodExecSession with write_stdin(), on_stdout() and friends. Incoming output is delivered while wait() or pump() runs.

Forward a pod port to a local one, like kubectl port-forward:

fwd <- pod_port_forward(k$client, "default", "nginx-abc", remote_port = 80)
httr2::request(paste0("http://127.0.0.1:", fwd$port)) |> httr2::req_perform()
fwd$close()

Both need the nanonext package. They verify the API server’s certificate against the kubeconfig CA (or the system CA bundle) and check its hostname, and authenticate with a bearer token. A kubeconfig whose user has only a client certificate, as kind, minikube and kubeadm create by default, gets an error explaining this; use a token instead:

# kubectl create serviceaccount rk8s-dev
# kubectl create clusterrolebinding rk8s-dev --clusterrole=edit \
#   --serviceaccount=default:rk8s-dev
cfg <- load_kube_config()
cfg$api_key <- list(authorization = paste(
  "Bearer", system("kubectl create token rk8s-dev", intern = TRUE)))
k <- kube(client = ApiClient$new(cfg))

Leader election

For controllers that need exactly one active replica:

run_as_leader(
  k$client,
  lease_name = "my-controller",
  lease_namespace = "kube-system",
  identity = paste0(Sys.info()[["nodename"]], "-", Sys.getpid()),
  on_started_leading = function(leader) {
    message("leading")
    repeat {
      leader$check()      # signals once leadership is lost
      reconcile_once()
      Sys.sleep(5)
    }
  },
  on_stopped_leading = function() message("stopped leading")
)

A background process (via callr) renews the lease. leader$check() signals an rk8s_leadership_lost condition as soon as the lease is taken or renewals stop succeeding; run_as_leader() then stops the callback, releases the lease and calls on_stopped_leading. Call it often, at least once per renew_deadline_seconds, so two replicas never act as leader at the same time. leader$is_leader() is the non-signalling version.

Errors

API failures surface as rk8s_api_error conditions whose $exception is an ApiException with the HTTP status, reason, headers, and parsed metav1.Status.

pod <- tryCatch(
  kube_get(k, "pod", "nope"),
  rk8s_api_error = function(e) {
    if (e$exception$status == 404L) NULL else stop(e)
  }
)

Dropping to the typed/generated layer

Any time kube_* doesn’t expose what you need, drop down. The verb client carries the underlying ApiClient and DynamicClient:

# Typed:
core <- CoreV1Api$new(k$client)
pods <- V1PodList$from_list(core$list_pod_for_all_namespaces())

# Or build a typed model explicitly:
dep <- V1Deployment$new(
  api_version = "apps/v1", kind = "Deployment",
  metadata = V1ObjectMeta$new(name = "nginx"),
  spec = V1DeploymentSpec$new(
    replicas = 3L,
    selector = V1LabelSelector$new(match_labels = list(app = "nginx")),
    template = V1PodTemplateSpec$new(
      metadata = V1ObjectMeta$new(labels = list(app = "nginx")),
      spec = V1PodSpec$new(containers = list(
        V1Container$new(name = "nginx", image = "nginx:1.25"))))))
AppsV1Api$new(k$client)$create_namespaced_deployment(
  namespace = "default", body = dep)

Regenerating from a newer Kubernetes spec 

curl -L -o tools/gen/spec/swagger.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/release-1.31/api/openapi-spec/swagger.json
Rscript tools/gen/generate.R tools/gen/spec/swagger.json R
R CMD build .

The generator (tools/gen/) reads OpenAPI v2 JSON and emits R6 model classes plus per-tag API classes — about 700 R files. NAMESPACE entries between sentinel lines are managed automatically.
